incentives.name: Class 17 qualified data center property tax treatment (as revised by HB 424)
incentives.summary: Reduced property tax classification for qualified data center property. HB 424 (signed May 13, 2025 per bill trackers) extended the construction window from 2027 to 2037, extended eligibility to wholly owned subsidiaries and parents, and taxes data-center-owned on-site generation at a reduced 0.9% rate for 10 years. Power sold from that generation to a utility or co-op is price-capped at production cost. Montana has no general state sales tax.

preemption.summary: Montana has no statute preempting local data center siting. The 2025 Right to Compute Act (SB 212) requires government restrictions on computational resources to be 'demonstrably necessary and narrowly tailored to fulfill a compelling government interest,' which counties say chills local regulation. Missoula County's county attorney said counties cannot permanently ban data centers but may use interim zoning for up to one year.

statutes.summary: Ties use of computational resources to constitutional property and free-expression rights; restrictions must meet a compelling-interest, narrowly tailored standard.

environmentalReview.summary: MEPA requires state agencies to prepare an environmental statement for major state actions significantly affecting Montana's environment. It applies only to state actions such as DEQ air permits or DNRC water decisions, not to private projects that need no state approval. A greenhouse gas assessment is optional, challenges must be filed within 60 days by prior commenters under a clear-and-convincing standard, and remedies are limited mostly to remand.

electricity.summary: NorthWestern Energy, a vertically integrated utility regulated by the elected Montana PSC, serves most of western and central Montana. Under Mont. Code Ann. 69-8-201, customers with 5 MW+ demand must show no long-term adverse impact on other customers. On about March 31, 2026, NorthWestern filed a Large New Load Tariff: 5-50 MW loads would get 5-year agreements with exit penalties, and loads over 50 MW would need 15-year minimum contracts, minimum usage and PSC approval of each contract. As of June 2026 nine entities had sought to intervene, and the case is likely to follow the PSC's ruling on the NorthWestern-Black Hills merger. HB 877 (2025), which would have limited PSC power to block service to large customers, died in the House.

incentives.name: ImagiNE Nebraska Act incentives (data centers)
incentives.summary: Nebraska's main business incentive program, offering tax credits and refunds. Executive Order 26-17 (signed July 20, 2026) ends data center access to ImagiNE incentives and prohibits approval of data center applications. Sen. Mike Jacobson plans legislation in 2027 to codify the change. Previously approved projects were reported as unaffected.

preemption.summary: No state statute preempts local data center siting; counties and municipalities control zoning, and at least 10 counties had moratoriums by mid-2026. State law instead regulates the utility relationship: Neb. Rev. Stat. 70-1506 (LB 526, 2025, amended by LB 1010, 2026) requires data centers to notify the local public power supplier, follow its interconnection rules, report annually and sign community benefit agreements. LB 1261 (2026) bars public power entities from condemning qualifying private generation co-located with 1,000 MW+ loads.

statutes.summary: Lets public power suppliers make data centers (10 MW+ peak demand) pay for the infrastructure upgrades they cause, after a load study. It also requires annual reports to DWEE and the Natural Resources Committee by Sept 30, decommissioning cost responsibility and a community benefit agreement.

Prohibits condemnation by consumer-owned suppliers of private generation co-located with 1,000 MW+ industrial loads that have Power Review Board approval and a long-term contract with a public power entity; excludes contracts executed after Dec 31, 2031.

electricity.summary: Nebraska is the only state served entirely by public power (NPPD, OPPD, LES, municipal utilities and rural districts), with no investor-owned utilities; it sits in SPP. These cover site control, backup generation evidence, financial commitments and a study fee of at least $50,000 or $1,000/MW, and let utilities set rates assigning system costs to large loads. LB 1261 lets hyperscale loads of 1,000 MW+ pair with private co-located generation under conditions.

incentives.name: Partial abatement of property and sales/use taxes for new or expanded data centers
incentives.summary: GOED may grant partial abatements of property (NRS ch. 361) and sales/use (NRS ch. 374) taxes. A tier of up to 10 years requires 10+ Nevada-resident employees and $25 million capex per county within 5 years. A 10-20 year tier requires 50+ employees and $100 million capex. Both tiers require 100% of the statewide average wage, health coverage and 50% Nevada-resident construction workers. Abating Local School Support Tax requires two-thirds Board approval, and 2025 legislation lets the GOED Board deny, reduce or condition abatements. EO 2026-005 (Sept 2026) requires new applicants to pay the Local School Support Tax in full and sign a binding Community Support Commitment.

incentives.name: Qualifying data center sales and use tax exemption
incentives.summary: Exempts electricity, electrical and cooling systems, emergency generators, servers, storage, network equipment, racks, software and related items bought for a comptroller-certified qualifying data center: at least 100,000 sq ft, one qualifying occupant, at least 20 qualifying jobs paying 120% of the county average weekly wage, and at least $200M invested over five years. The exemption lasts 10 years (15 years at $250M or more), excludes local sales taxes, and is barred for data centers with a former Ch. 313 value-limitation agreement. Last amended by HB 1620 (2025, eff. Sept. 1, 2025), an apparent nonsubstantive code update. On Sept. 21, 2026, Gov. Abbott said he will work with the Legislature to eliminate financial incentives for data centers, so the exemption is at risk in the 2027 session.

preemption.summary: Texas has no data-center-specific preemption statute. Local leverage is weak by design. Zoning power under LGC ch. 211 belongs to municipalities and applies inside city limits. Counties have no general zoning authority: ch. 231 allows county zoning only in listed areas (Padre Island, Amistad, military zones, certain lakes, El Paso Mission Trail, Hood County), and ch. 232 limits counties mainly to subdivision platting. SB 2038 (2023, LGC 42.101-42.105) lets residents or majority-in-value landowners petition out of a city's ETJ, further reducing city development controls around unincorporated sites. Cities can still zone data centers inside their limits. In 2026, statewide constraints shifted to state executive action: the Aug. 3 ERCOT/PUCT audit with denial of interconnection for failing projects, and the Sept. 21 TCEQ permit halt.

electricity.summary: Most of the state is in ERCOT under PUCT jurisdiction. SB 6 (2025, eff. June 20, 2025) created PURA 37.0561 large-load interconnection standards for loads of 75 MW or more: a study fee of at least $100,000, duplicate-request disclosure, site control and financial security. It also requires curtailment capability during load shed for loads interconnected after Dec. 31, 2025, an ERCOT demand-reduction service, ERCOT-directed switching to backup generation in emergencies, PUCT review of co-location deals with existing generators, and a 4CP transmission cost-allocation review with rules due by Dec. 31, 2026. The PUCT adopted 16 TAC 25.194 on Sept. 18, 2026. Gov. Abbott's Aug. 3, 2026 directive requires an audit of all data centers in ERCOT's queue (about 474 GW of requests, roughly 90% data centers) and denial of interconnection for failing projects. ERCOT is targeting a report by Dec. 10, 2026 and has said Batch Zero study results will not be done by April 9, 2027.

incentives.name: High impact data center property tax regime (tax increment distribution)
incentives.summary: Covers data centers with 90 MW or more of aggregate critical IT load placed in service on or after July 1, 2025. The Board of Public Works values the property, which is taxed at ordinary levy rates; PILOTs and TIF are barred. The tax increment above base value is split 50% to the Personal Income Tax Reduction Fund, 30% to the situs county, 10% to all counties per capita, 5% to the Economic Enhancement Grant Fund (Water Development Authority), and 5% to the Electric Grid Stabilization and Security Fund. This is a revenue-distribution framework rather than a tax break.

preemption.summary: Strong statutory preemption for certified projects. Under W. Va. Code 5B-2-21b (HB 2014, passed April 12, 2025, effective July 11, 2025), counties and municipalities may not limit in any way the creation, operation or expansion of certified microgrid districts or high impact data centers, notwithstanding home rule. These projects are exempt from county and municipal zoning, horticultural, noise, viewshed, lighting, development and land-use ordinances; from local building permitting, inspection and code enforcement; from local licenses; and from local legal jurisdiction except as the article provides. The statute sets no replacement setback, noise or light standards. Projects must still pay municipal B&O and property taxes, pay local service fees, and build to the State Building Code. HB 4983 (approved March 27, 2026) authorized the Commerce certification rule. Democrats said in June 2026 they will keep pushing to restore local authority.
